title: JavaScript Basics
summary: Learn the JavaScript a page needs, from zero: values, variables, decisions, functions, objects, arrays, and loops, tried in the browser's Console.
intro: HTML says what's on a page and CSS says how it looks, but neither can change anything once the page has loaded. A button that adds an item to a cart, a form that warns you before it sends, a list that fills in with fresh results: each of those needs a program, and in the browser, programs are written in **JavaScript**. This lesson starts from zero. It covers what a program is, where you write JavaScript and see what it does, and the pieces every script is built from: values, variables, decisions, functions, objects, arrays, and loops. That's everything the next two lessons use to change pages and talk to servers. When you want more depth, Hack University's Learn JavaScript course teaches the whole language, with problems to solve.

steps.title: What a program is, and where it runs
steps.body:
Before you can write JavaScript, you need two things: an idea of what a program is, and a place to type one and watch it work. This part gives you both, so you can try every example in this lesson as you read.

## A program is a list of steps

A **program** is a list of instructions for a computer, written in a language it can follow. It works like a recipe: the steps go in order, from the top down, and each one is done before the next begins. The text of a program is called **code**, and when the computer follows the steps, it **runs** the program.

In JavaScript, each instruction is a **statement**. A statement usually fits on one line and ends with a semicolon, like this one, which asks the browser to show a message:

```javascript
console.log("Hello!");
```

`console.log` means: write this in the Console, which comes next. The text in quotes is the message. The brackets after `console.log` hold what you give it, and the semicolon ends the statement.

JavaScript is the one programming language every browser can run. Each browser has a **JavaScript engine** built in, the part that reads your code and carries it out, which the lesson on how a browser draws a page named. The same language also runs outside the browser, in Node.js, the program you checked the version of in the first lesson. This course uses it in the browser.

## The Console

The **Console** is a panel in the browser's DevTools where you can type JavaScript and see the answer at once. Open DevTools with F12, or with Command, Option, and I on a Mac, and click the **Console** tab. You'll see a prompt, a `>` sign with a blinking cursor.

Type `2 + 3` and press Enter. The Console answers `5`. Type `console.log("Hello!")` and press Enter, and it prints Hello!. A gray `undefined` appears under it too. That's the Console showing what the statement handed back, which for `console.log` is nothing, and you can ignore it.

The first time you paste code into Chrome's Console, it refuses and asks you to type `allow pasting` first. That's a guard against scams: people get tricked into pasting code that takes over their accounts. Type it, then paste. Only ever paste code you understand, like the code in these lessons.

The Console is for trying things. Whatever you type there disappears when you reload the page.

## Code in a page

To keep code, put it in the page. The `script` element holds JavaScript, and the browser runs it when it reaches that point in the HTML:

```html
<script>
  console.log("Hello from the page!");
</script>
```

Most code goes in a file of its own instead, ending in `.js`, and the page loads it with the `src` attribute, the same way an `img` loads a picture:

```html
<script src="app.js"></script>
```

A separate file keeps the HTML readable, lets several pages share one script, and lets the browser keep a copy instead of downloading it on every page. For now, put the `script` element at the very end of the page, after everything else. The next lesson explains why that matters, and a better way.

Anything a script prints with `console.log` shows up in the Console of that page, with the file's name and the line number on the right, like `app.js:2`. That's how you'll check what your code is doing, all through this course.

## Comments

A line that starts with `//` is a **comment**: a note for people, which the browser skips. Comments explain why code does something, not what it does, since the code already says that.

```javascript
// Prices are in cents, so 450 is 4.50.
const price = 450;
```

## When something goes wrong

Computers follow code exactly. One wrong letter, like `consol` for `console`, and the browser can't run the line. It stops the script there and shows an **error** in the Console, in red: what kind of mistake it was, what it couldn't understand, and the file and line it was on. Every programmer sees errors every day. Read them: the message usually says exactly what's wrong, and the line number says where.

Capital letters count too. `console.Log` with a capital L is a different name from `console.log`, and it's an error.

To try this lesson's examples, make a folder in the Playground with an `index.html` and an `app.js`, start Python's server in it, the way the How the Web Works lessons did, and open the page with the Console showing.

examples.title: A page that loads a script
examples.prompt: A whole page, saved as index.html, in a folder in the Playground. The script element loads app.js from the same folder.
examples.code: Open the Console to see what app.js prints.
examples.explanation: The browser reads the page from the top. It shows the heading, then reaches the `script` element, downloads `app.js` from the same folder, and runs it from its first line to its last. The `src` value is a relative path, from the How the Web Works lessons, so `app.js` means the file next to this page. Every example in this lesson is a script you can paste into `app.js`: save it, reload the page, and read what it printed in the Console. Python's server sends `app.js` like any other file, so you'll see a request for it in the terminal each time you reload.

examples.title: Statements run in order
examples.prompt: Three statements in app.js. Reload the page, and this is what the Console shows.
examples.output:
Hello!
This page has a script.
5
examples.explanation: The lines print in the order they're written, top to bottom, because that's the order the browser runs them. The first two give `console.log` text in quotes, and it prints the text without the quotes. The quotes only mark where the text starts and ends. The third gives it `2 + 3`, with no quotes, so the browser works out the sum first and prints the answer, 5. Put quotes around it, as `"2 + 3"`, and it would print the characters 2 + 3 instead, since in quotes it's just text. Next to each line in the Console, on the right, you'll see `app.js` and the line number it came from.

examples.title: An error stops the script
examples.prompt: The same kind of script, with a typo on the second line.
examples.output:
Before the mistake
Uncaught ReferenceError: consol is not defined
examples.explanation: The first line runs and prints. The second asks for something called `consol`, and nothing has that name, so the browser stops with a **ReferenceError**: a name it doesn't know. Uncaught means no code was set up to handle the problem, so the script ends right there. The third line never runs, which is why After the mistake is missing. In the Console, the red message also shows `app.js` and line 2 on the right, so you know where to look. When a page does nothing at all, a red error early in a script is often why: nothing after it ran.

steps.title: Values and variables
steps.body:
Every program works with information: a name, a price, how many items are in a cart, whether a box is ticked. Each piece of information is a **value**, and a **variable** gives a value a name, so the program can use it again, and change it. Almost every line of code you'll write uses both.

## Kinds of value

JavaScript has a few basic kinds of value, called **types**. Three cover most of what you'll use:

- A **string** is text, written in quotes: `"Lake Loop"`. Double quotes and single quotes, `'Lake Loop'`, mean the same thing. Pick one and stick to it.
- A **number** is a number, whole or not: `42`, `5.5`, `-3`. No quotes, since `"42"` in quotes is a string that happens to hold digits.
- A **boolean** is one of two values, `true` or `false`, with no quotes. It answers a yes-or-no question, like whether dogs are allowed.

Two more mean no value. `undefined` means nothing was ever given, like a variable you named but never filled. `null` means empty on purpose, like a search that found nothing. You'll meet both when something is missing.

`typeof` tells you a value's type, which helps when something behaves strangely: `typeof 42` is `"number"` and `typeof "42"` is `"string"`.

## Variables

A variable is a name that refers to a value. You make one with `const` or `let`, then a name, an equals sign, and the value:

```javascript
const trailName = "Lake Loop";
let visitors = 0;
```

The `=` here doesn't mean equals, as it does in math. It means **assign**: make this name refer to this value. From then on, writing `trailName` means `"Lake Loop"`.

```diagram javascript-basics-variables
Each name refers to a value. A let name can be pointed at a new value later, and a const name can't.
```

- `const` makes a name that always refers to the same value. Trying to assign it again is an error.
- `let` makes a name you can assign again later, like a counter that goes up.

Use `const` unless you know the value will change. Then a reader knows at a glance which names stay put. You'll also see `var` in older code. It's the original way to make variables, with some surprising rules, and new code doesn't use it.

The diagram shows two names: `trailName` refers to a string and stays that way, and `visitors` started at 0 and was later given 1. Assigning a new value doesn't change the old one: the name just refers to something else now.

## Naming

Names can hold letters, digits, `_`, and `$`, but can't start with a digit, and can't be one of JavaScript's own words, like `let` or `if`, which are called **keywords**. Capitals count, so `total` and `Total` are two different names. JavaScript code uses **camelCase**: run the words together and capitalize each one after the first, as in `trailName` or `itemsInCart`. Choose names that say what the value is. `cartTotal` tells a reader something, and `x` doesn't.

## Math with numbers

Numbers use the **operators** you know, the symbols that work on values: `+`, `-`, `*` for times, and `/` for divide. `%` gives the remainder after dividing, so `7 % 2` is 1, which tells you whether a number is odd. Brackets come first, as in math: `(2 + 3) * 4` is 20.

To change a variable based on its own value, assign it again:

```javascript
let visitors = 0;
visitors = visitors + 1;
visitors += 5;
visitors++;
```

The second line reads: take the value of `visitors`, add 1, and make `visitors` refer to that. `visitors += 5` is short for `visitors = visitors + 5`, and `visitors++` adds 1. After all three, `visitors` is 7.

One surprise to know about: a computer stores most decimal numbers almost, not exactly, so `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`. For money, count in whole cents, and turn them into euros or dollars only to show them.

## Joining strings

`+` also joins strings, one after another: `"Hello, " + "Sam"` gives `"Hello, Sam"`. A neater way is a **template literal**, a string in backticks, where `${}` drops a value into the text:

```javascript
const visitor = "Sam";
const greeting = `Hello, ${visitor}!`;
```

`greeting` is `"Hello, Sam!"`. Any code can go between the curly brackets, like `${visitors + 1}`.

## Strings that look like numbers

Here's a trap you'll fall into on your first form. If either side of `+` is a string, JavaScript joins instead of adding, so `"3" + 1` is `"31"`, not 4. Text a person types into a page always arrives as a string, even when it's digits. `Number("3")` turns the string into the number 3, and then `+` adds as you'd expect. If the string isn't a number at all, like `Number("three")`, you get `NaN`, short for not a number, which is JavaScript's way of saying the math made no sense.

examples.title: Three kinds of value
examples.prompt: A string, a number, and a boolean, each stored under a name, then used and checked with typeof.
examples.explanation: The first three lines make three variables with `const`, since none of them will change. The first `console.log` prints the value `trailName` refers to. The second shows that a variable can go anywhere its value could: `lengthKm * 2` is `5.5 * 2`, so it prints 11. The last line gives `console.log` three values, separated by commas, and it prints them all on one line with spaces between them. Each `typeof` gives back the type's name as a string: a string, a number, and a boolean. Giving `console.log` several values like this is handy for printing a label and a value together, as in `console.log("Length:", lengthKm)`.

examples.title: Changing a let, and trying to change a const
examples.prompt: A counter made with let goes up three times. Then the script tries to give a const a new value.
examples.output:
12
Uncaught TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
examples.explanation: `steps` starts at 0, goes to 1, then to 11 with `+= 10`, then to 12 with `++`, and the first `console.log` prints 12. Then `city` is made with `const`, so assigning `"Porto"` to it is an error: a **TypeError**, the error for using a value in a way it doesn't allow. The script stops, so the last line never runs. This error is useful. It means a name you said would never change is about to, which is usually a mistake somewhere. If the value really does need to change, make it with `let` instead.

examples.title: A string that looks like a number
examples.prompt: A number of tickets arrives as the string "3", the way text from a form field would. Adding to it goes wrong until it's turned into a number.
examples.explanation: `tickets` is a string, because of the quotes, so `tickets + 1` joins a 1 onto the end and prints 31. `Number(tickets)` turns the string into the number 3, and then `+` adds, so the next line prints 4. The template literal drops two values into one sentence: the visitor's name and the total. Template literals turn whatever goes in `${}` into text, so numbers work there too. The last line is the decimal surprise: 0.1 and 0.2 can't be stored exactly, so the sum comes out a tiny bit off. When you show a number like that to people, you round it first, and when it's money, you count in cents to begin with.

steps.title: Comparisons and decisions

examples.title: Choosing one of three messages
examples.prompt: An if, an else if, and an else pick advice for a walk by the temperature.
examples.explanation: The browser checks the conditions from the top. `31 >= 30` is `true`, so it runs the first block and skips the other two entirely, even though `31 >= 15` is true as well. That's why the order matters: put the most specific question first. Change `temperature` to 20, and the first condition is `false`, the second is `true`, and it prints the mild message. At 5, both are `false` and the `else` block runs. Without the `else`, a cold day would print nothing at all, which is sometimes what you want and sometimes a bug.

examples.title: What comparisons answer
examples.prompt: Each line prints the answer to one comparison or logical operator.
examples.output:
true
false
true
true
false
true
false
examples.explanation: Every comparison gives back a boolean, which `console.log` prints. `"5" === 5` is `false` because a string and a number are different types, even with the same digit. `"5" == 5` is `true` because `==` turns the string into a number first, and that quiet conversion is the reason to avoid it. `3 !== 4` is `true` since they differ. `10 > 3 && 2 > 5` is `false`, since `&&` needs both sides and the second is `false`. With `||`, one `true` side is enough. `!true` flips to `false`.

examples.title: Checking whether anything is there
examples.prompt: Two checks that use truthy and falsy values: an empty search box, and an empty cart.
examples.output:
Type something to search.
Your cart is empty.
examples.explanation: `searchText` is an empty string, which is falsy, so the `if` treats it as `false` and the `else` block asks for a search. Put any text in the quotes, even one letter, and it becomes truthy and the first message prints instead. `itemsInCart` is 0, which is falsy too, so it prints that the cart is empty. Here, treating 0 as nothing is exactly right. In a page, `searchText` would come from what someone typed in a search box, which the next lesson shows how to read, and this is the check you'd run before searching.

steps.title: Functions

examples.title: A function that works something out
examples.prompt: A function that returns the shipping cost for a cart total, called with two totals, then used inside a sum.
examples.explanation: The first call hands in 42, so `total` is 42 during that call, the condition is `false`, and the function returns 5, which `console.log` prints. The second call hands in 80, so `return 0` runs and ends the function there. The last line calls it inside a template literal: `shippingCost(cart)` becomes 5, and `cart + 5` is 47. Notice the argument doesn't have to be called `total` outside: here it's `cart`, and inside the function the same value is known as `total`. A function like this is easy to test, since the same argument always gives back the same answer.

examples.title: A callback that runs later
examples.prompt: An arrow function used straight away, then another one handed to setTimeout, which calls it a second later.
examples.output:
42
Asking the browser to wait one second...
This line runs before the timer.
One second later!
examples.explanation: `double(21)` returns 42 straight away. Then `setTimeout` gets two arguments: an arrow function and 1000 milliseconds. It doesn't pause the script. It hands the function to the browser and returns at once, so the next line prints before the timer's message, even though it comes later in the file. About a second after that, the browser calls the arrow function, and One second later! appears last. Code that runs later, when something happens, is how everything interactive on the web works, and the next lesson shows how the browser decides when to run it.

examples.title: A name that only exists inside
examples.prompt: A function makes a variable inside its body. Code outside the function tries to use it.
examples.output:
Welcome, Ana!
Uncaught ReferenceError: message is not defined
examples.explanation: The call `greet("Ana")` runs the body with `visitor` as `"Ana"`, makes `message` inside it, and returns its value, which prints. Once the function has returned, `message` is gone: it only ever existed inside that function. So the last line asks for a name that doesn't exist out here, and the browser stops with the same ReferenceError a typo gives. To use a value a function made, use what it returns, as the first `console.log` does. You could store it in a variable of your own, even one also called `message`, and the two would never clash.

steps.title: Objects
steps.body:
Real things have several details at once. A trail has a name, a length, and a rule about dogs. A person has a name and an email. An **object** keeps all of a thing's details together under one name. Objects matter even more in the browser, because the browser gives you everything as objects: the page is an object called `document`, and the Console is an object called `console`.

## Making an object

An object is written in curly brackets, as a list of **properties**, each a name, a colon, and a value, with commas between them:

```javascript
const trail = {
  name: "Lake Loop",
  lengthKm: 5,
  dogsAllowed: true,
};
```

The comma after the last property is optional, and many teams leave it in, so adding a property later only changes one line.

## Reading and changing properties

A dot reads a property: `trail.name` is `"Lake Loop"`. The same dot, with `=`, changes one, or adds a new one:

```javascript
trail.lengthKm = 5.5;
trail.difficulty = "easy";
```

Square brackets with a string do the same as a dot: `trail["name"]`. You need them when the property's name is in a variable, as in `trail[detail]`, where `detail` holds the name.

Notice that `trail` was made with `const`, and its properties still changed. `const` only means the name always refers to the same object. What's inside the object can change. That's how most of the objects the browser gives you work: the same `document` all along, with contents that change.

Asking for a property that isn't there gives `undefined`, not an error. Going one step further does give an error: if `trail.start` is `undefined`, then `trail.start.lat` asks `undefined` for a property, and you get a **TypeError** saying it cannot read properties of `undefined`. You'll see the same message with `null` in the next lesson, when code looks for something on the page that isn't there. When you do, look at the thing before the last dot: that's the one that's missing.

## Objects inside objects

A property's value can be anything, another object included:

```javascript
const trail = {
  name: "Lake Loop",
  start: { lat: 38.72, lng: -9.14 },
};
```

Dots chain, one step at a time: `trail.start.lat` is 38.72.

## Methods

A property's value can be a function too. A function that belongs to an object is called a **method**, and you call it with a dot and round brackets. You've used one since the first part: `console.log` is the `log` method of the `console` object.

Strings and numbers have methods too, even though they aren't objects you made:

- `"Lake Loop".toUpperCase()` gives `"LAKE LOOP"`.
- `"Lake Loop".includes("Lake")` gives `true`.
- `"  sam@example.com ".trim()` gives `"sam@example.com"`, with the spaces at both ends removed, which is handy for anything typed into a form.

Some properties aren't methods, just values. `"Lake Loop".length` is 9, the number of characters, with no brackets, since it's not something you call.

JavaScript also comes with ready-made objects full of methods. `Math` holds math: `Math.round(5.6)` is 6, `Math.max(3, 8)` is 8, and `Math.random()` gives a random number between 0 and 1.

## Looking at an object in the Console

When you give `console.log` a whole object, as in `console.log(trail)`, the Console shows it on one line in curly brackets, with a small triangle in front. Click the triangle and it opens, showing each property on a line of its own. It's the quickest way to see what's inside an object, and you'll use it on the browser's objects all the time. Try `console.log(document)` on any page.

examples.title: Reading and changing a trail
examples.prompt: An object with three properties. The script reads two of them, changes one, adds one, and asks for one that doesn't exist.
examples.output:
Lake Loop
5
Lake Loop: 5.5 km, easy
undefined
examples.explanation: `trail.name` and `trail["lengthKm"]` read two properties, one with a dot and one with square brackets, which do the same job. Then the script changes `lengthKm` and adds `difficulty`, a property that didn't exist before, just by assigning it. Both work even though `trail` is a `const`, because the name still refers to the same object. The template literal reads three properties into one sentence. The last line asks for `elevation`, which the object doesn't have, and gets `undefined` rather than an error. Mistyping a property's name gives `undefined` the same way, so when a value comes out `undefined`, check the spelling first.

examples.title: Methods on strings, and objects you already know
examples.prompt: A string's length and two of its methods, a method from Math, and a look at what console and console.log are.
examples.explanation: `length` is a property, so it has no brackets: 9 characters, the space included. `toUpperCase()` and `includes()` are methods, so they have brackets, and `includes` takes an argument, the text to look for. Neither changes `trailName`: `toUpperCase()` returns a new string, and `trailName` still refers to the original. `Math.round(5.6)` calls the `round` method of the `Math` object and gives 6. The last line shows what you've been using all along: `console` is an object, and its `log` property is a function, which is what makes it a method.

examples.title: Asking a missing object for a property
examples.prompt: The trail has no start property. The script reads it, then tries to read a property of what it got.
examples.output:
undefined
Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'lat')
examples.explanation: `trail.start` doesn't exist, so it's `undefined`, and the first line prints that. The second line asks `undefined` for its `lat` property, but `undefined` isn't an object and has no properties, so the browser stops with a TypeError. The message says exactly what happened: it tried to read `lat` from `undefined`. That tells you to look one step back, at `trail.start`, which is the missing piece. This is the error you'll see more than any other in browser code, usually with `null` in place of `undefined`, when a script looks for something on the page that isn't there.

steps.title: Arrays and loops
steps.body:
Lists are everywhere on the web: search results, the items in a cart, messages in a chat, the trails on a map. An **array** holds a list of values in order, and a **loop** runs the same steps once for each one. Together they let a few lines of code handle a list of any length.

## Arrays

An array is written in square brackets, with commas between its values:

```javascript
const trails = ["Lake Loop", "Ridge Trail", "North Loop"];
```

Each value has a number for its place, called its **index**, and the count starts at 0, not 1. So `trails[0]` is `"Lake Loop"` and `trails[2]` is `"North Loop"`. Starting at 0 trips everyone up at first: the first item is index 0, and the last is one less than the number of items.

```diagram javascript-basics-array
An array numbers its items from 0. Each item here is an object with properties of its own.
```

`trails.length` is how many items there are, 3, so the last one is always `trails[trails.length - 1]`. An index past the end, like `trails[3]`, gives `undefined`.

Arrays come with methods:

- `trails.push("Cliff Path")` adds an item to the end.
- `trails.includes("Ridge Trail")` is `true` when the item is in the array.
- `trails.indexOf("North Loop")` gives its index, 2, or -1 when it isn't there.
- `trails.join(", ")` gives one string with all the items, separated by what you pass.

An array can hold any values, and an array of objects is the most common list of all. The diagram shows one: each item is a trail object with its own name and length, so `trails[1].name` is `"Ridge Trail"`. A list of search results, or of products, arrives from a server in exactly this shape.

## for...of: once for each item

A **loop** repeats a block. The one you'll use most for arrays is `for...of`, which runs its block once for each item, in order, with a name for the current one:

```javascript
for (const trail of trails) {
  console.log(trail);
}
```

Read it as: for each trail of trails, run this block. The first time round, `trail` is the first item, the next time the second, and so on to the end. Each time round is called an **iteration**.

## Loops with a counter

Sometimes you need the index, or a loop that isn't over an array. The classic `for` loop has three parts in its brackets: a starting step, a condition to keep going, and a step after each round:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  console.log(`Round ${i}`);
}
```

It makes `i` as 0, runs the block while `i < 3` is `true`, and adds 1 after each round, so it prints rounds 0, 1, and 2. A `while` loop is simpler: `while (condition) { ... }` repeats its block as long as the condition stays `true`. Make sure something in the block changes the condition. A loop that never ends freezes the whole page, as the next lesson explains.

## Methods that take a function

Arrays have methods that take a callback, a function they call once for each item. They say what you want done, in fewer lines than a loop:

- `trails.filter((trail) => trail.dogsAllowed)` gives a new array of just the items for which the function returns `true`.
- `trails.map((trail) => trail.name)` gives a new array with the function's answer for each item, here just the names.
- `trails.find((trail) => trail.lengthKm < 6)` gives the first item for which the function returns `true`, or `undefined` if none does.
- `trails.forEach((trail) => console.log(trail.name))` calls the function for each item, like a `for...of` loop.

`filter` and `map` don't change the original array. They return a new one, which makes them safe to use on data you need again.

## What comes next

That's the JavaScript the rest of this course uses. The next lesson points it at the page: finding elements, changing them, and running functions when people click and type. Hack University's **Learn JavaScript** course goes much deeper into the language itself, with practice problems for each idea: classes, errors, JSON, waiting for things that take time, and more. It runs its programs in Node.js, not in a page, but the language is the same, so everything you learn there works here.

examples.title: An array of names
examples.prompt: An array of three trail names, read by index, measured with length, then given one more item.
examples.output:
Lake Loop
North Loop
3
North Loop
undefined
4 true
examples.explanation: Index 0 is the first item and index 2 the third. `length` is 3, so `trails.length - 1` is 2, the last index, which gives the last item however long the array is. `trails[3]` asks for a fourth item that doesn't exist, and gets `undefined`, the same as a missing property. `push` adds Cliff Path to the end, even though `trails` is a `const`: like an object, the array is the same one, with new contents. After that, the length is 4 and `includes` finds the new item, and `console.log` prints both on one line.

examples.title: Adding up a cart with a loop
examples.prompt: A cart is an array of objects. A for...of loop prints each item and adds its price to a running total.
examples.output:
Water bottle: 12
Trail map: 6
Snack bar: 2
Total: 20
examples.explanation: `total` starts at 0 and is made with `let`, since it changes. The loop runs three times. Each time, `item` is the next object in the cart, so `item.name` and `item.price` read that object's properties, and `total += item.price` adds its price. After the loop, the total line runs once and prints 20. Running totals like this one, a variable before the loop that each round adds to, are one of the most common shapes of code there is. Add a fourth item to the array, and the same loop handles it, with no other change.

examples.title: Filtering and mapping a list
examples.prompt: From a list of trail objects, keep the ones that allow dogs, turn those into a list of names, then find the first short trail.
examples.output:
Lake Loop, North Loop
Lake Loop
examples.explanation: `filter` calls the arrow function once for each trail, and keeps the trails for which it returns `true`. `trail.dogsAllowed` is already a boolean, so Ridge Trail drops out. `map` then turns each kept trail into its name, giving an array of two strings, and `join` makes them one string with a comma and a space between. `find` stops at the first trail shorter than 6 km and returns that whole object, so `short.name` reads its name. `trails` itself is untouched by all three. The next lesson uses `filter` and `map` the same way to decide which items to show on a page.

recap:
- A program is a list of statements that run in order, top to bottom, and an error stops it at the line where it happened.
- Try code in the Console, and keep it in a .js file that the page loads with a script element.
- Values are strings, numbers, booleans, undefined, and null, and const or let gives a value a name.
- Text that looks like a number is still a string, so turn it into a number before you add to it.
- Compare with === and !==, and use if, else if, and else to choose what runs.
- A function takes arguments, runs its body, and returns a value, and a callback is a function you hand to someone else to call later.
- Objects group properties under one name, and a method is a function that belongs to an object.
- Arrays hold lists from index 0, for...of runs a block for each item, and filter, map, and find take callbacks.
